title: Structural Organisation in Animals
tagline: From tissues to organ systems: the earthworm, cockroach and frog as the standard specimens.

overview.intro: Having sorted animals into phyla, the course now asks how an animal body is built from the inside out: tissues first, then how tissues form organs and organ systems, and then the anatomy of the three specimens that the syllabus names for practical study — the earthworm, the cockroach and the frog. This chapter explains the four animal tissues and the principles of organ-system organisation, and then works through the digestive, circulatory, nervous and excretory systems of each specimen so that the anatomy can be described rather than merely listed. Practicals and identification questions dominate this area: label a diagram, name the tissue under a slide, or describe the path of food through the alimentary canal.

facts.label: Four tissue types
facts.value: Epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues, each with a characteristic structure and function.

facts.label: Earthworm segments
facts.value: About 100 to 120 segments, with the clitellum around segments 14 to 16 and nephridia in almost every segment.

facts.label: Cockroach spiracles
facts.value: Ten pairs along the thorax and abdomen open into a network of tracheae that carry air directly to the tissues.

facts.label: Frog heart
facts.value: Three chambers, two atria and one ventricle, with a thin-walled sinus venosus receiving blood from the body.

learningOutcomes: Describe the four animal tissues with structure, function and example location.
Explain how tissues are organised into organs and organ systems.
Describe the alimentary canal, circulation and excretion of the earthworm.
Outline the external features, respiration and nervous system of the cockroach.
Describe the digestive, circulatory and nervous systems of the frog.

blocks.text: Tissue is a group of cells similar in structure and origin that work together to perform a particular function, and the four animal tissue types explain most of what an organ does. Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces, lines cavities and glands, and is classified by the number of layers and by cell shape: simple squamous, a single layer of flat cells such as the alveoli of the lung where thin walls permit rapid diffusion; stratified squamous, many layers protecting surfaces subject to abrasion such as the skin; cuboidal, forming glands and the kidney tubules; columnar, lining the intestine with microvilli for absorption; and ciliated columnar, with cilia that sweep mucus along as in the trachea. Epithelia rest on a basement membrane and are avascular, receiving nutrients from the underlying connective tissue, and they divide rapidly to replace worn cells. Connective tissue is the most abundant and widely distributed, with cells scattered through a matrix that they secrete, and its forms differ by the nature of that matrix: loose areolar tissue packs organs and gives flexibility; adipose tissue stores fat and insulates; dense regular tendons and ligaments attach muscle to bone and bone to bone; cartilage is firm yet elastic and supports the ear and nose; bone is rigid through calcium salts and forms the skeleton; blood has a liquid plasma matrix and carries oxygen and nutrients; and lymph is a tissue fluid draining back into the circulatory system. Muscle tissue is specialised for contraction and comes in three forms: skeletal striated muscle attached to bones under voluntary control, with long multinucleated fibres and visible striations; cardiac muscle of the heart, branching and striated yet involuntary and resistant to fatigue; and smooth muscle in the walls of hollow organs such as the intestine and blood vessels, uninucleate, spindle-shaped, involuntary and able to sustain slow contraction. Nervous tissue carries impulses rapidly over long distances: the neuron is the structural unit, with a cell body containing a large nucleus, branching dendrites receiving impulses and a single long axon carrying them away, and neuroglia cells support and protect the neurons. The four tissues combine into organs, so that the stomach, for example, is epithelium lining and secreting, muscle in its wall for churning, connective tissue as its layers and blood supply, and nervous tissue in its plexuses coordinating the movement.

items: Tissue: cells of similar structure and origin working together on one function.
Epithelial tissue covers and lines, is avascular and classified by layers and cell shape.
Connective tissue has cells in a matrix they secrete: areolar, adipose, tendon, cartilage, bone, blood and lymph.
Muscle tissue contracts: skeletal voluntary striated, cardiac involuntary striated and branching, smooth involuntary spindle-shaped.
Nervous tissue conducts impulses; the neuron with dendrites, cell body and axon is its unit.
Organs combine several tissues, and organ systems combine organs for a shared function.
Rapid cell division and an avascular nature are two features that identify epithelia.

items.text: Why tendons are dense and regular
items.note: Collagen fibres aligned parallel to the pull transmit the force of the muscle to the bone without stretching.

blocks.text: The earthworm is the standard annelid specimen, and its anatomy illustrates how segmentation organises an animal body. The body is long and cylindrical with 100 to 120 segments, each separated internally by a septum, and the first segment bears the prostomium, a lobe overhanging the mouth. Segments 14 to 16 are swollen into the clitellum, which secretes the cocoon in which eggs develop. Externally each segment carries setae, small bristles that grip the soil, and the mouth lies in the first segment with the prostomium above it. Food passes in a straight line: mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, crop for storage, gizzard for grinding with the help of swallowed sand, intestine, and anus, with the typhlosole — a fold of the intestinal wall — increasing the absorptive surface. The earthworm has a closed circulatory system with two main lateral hearts, or aortic arches, in segments 7 to 11 that pump blood dorsally, a dorsal vessel carrying blood backwards and a ventral vessel carrying it forwards, and capillaries feeding every segment; its blood contains haemoglobin dissolved in the plasma. Excretion is by nephridia, coiled tubules present in nearly every segment that open to the outside by a nephridiopore, making the earthworm a metanephridiate animal. The nervous system consists of a bilobed cerebral ganglion, the brain, on the pharynx, a circum-pharyngeal ring and a double ventral nerve cord with segmental ganglia, so the worm retains a simple reflex arc. Respiration occurs through the moist body wall, where dissolved oxygen diffuses into the blood capillaries, which is why an earthworm dies when its skin dries.

items: Body of 100 to 120 metameres with setae for grip and a prostomium overhanging the mouth.
Clitellum on segments 14 to 16 secretes the cocoon in which the embryos develop.
Alimentary canal: mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, crop, gizzard, intestine with typhlosole, anus.
Closed circulation with aortic arches in segments 7 to 11, dorsal and ventral vessels and haemoglobin in the plasma.
Excretion by paired nephridia in almost every segment, opening by a nephridiopore.
Respiration through the moist body wall, so the animal must stay damp to survive.
Nervous system: cerebral ganglia, circum-pharyngeal connectives and a ventral nerve cord with segmental ganglia.

items.note: The muscular gizzard has no teeth, so the grains swallowed with soil grind the organic matter against its wall.
Each segment’s muscles and setae act under the segmental ganglia, so local stimulation produces a local response even before the brain is involved.

blocks.text: The cockroach is the standard arthropod specimen, with a body divided into head, thorax and abdomen and enclosed in a chitinous exoskeleton. The head bears a pair of compound eyes, a pair of thread-like antennae and mouthparts adapted for chewing — a labrum, mandibles, maxillae and labium with a maxillary palp — and it is joined to the thorax by a flexible neck. The thorax carries three pairs of jointed legs and two pairs of wings, the leathery tegmina in front and membranous hind wings behind, and the abdomen ends in a pair of anal cerci. Respiration is by tracheae: ten pairs of spiracles on the thorax and abdomen open into larger tracheal tubes that branch into fine tracheoles reaching each tissue, so air reaches the cells directly without the blood carrying it. The alimentary canal runs mouth to anus with a crop for storage and a gizzard for grinding, and nitrogenous waste is removed by Malpighian tubules that empty into the gut — the insect answer to the excretory problem. The nervous system mirrors the earthworm’s, with a supra-esophageal ganglion, a circum-pharyngeal ring and a ventral nerve cord with ganglia in each segment, while the sense organs include the compound eyes, antennae for touch and smell, and cerci sensitive to air movements. The frog, as an amphibian, shows the same systems in a vertebrate plan: the alimentary canal begins at the mouth with a sticky tongue for catching insects, passes through the oesophagus, stomach, small intestine with a fat body, large intestine and cloaca, with bile from the liver and juice from the pancreas entering the first part of the small intestine. Its three-chambered heart lies in a pericardium and receives blood through a sinus venosus, while a double circulation sends blood to the skin, lungs and body. The frog breathes through the buccal cavity by buccal pumping as well as through its moist skin, its kidneys are paired mesonephric structures with ureters opening into the cloaca, and its nervous system comprises a brain in a cranium, spinal cord and ten pairs of cranial nerves.

items: Cockroach: head, thorax and abdomen in a chitinous exoskeleton with compound eyes and chewing mouthparts.
Thorax bears three pairs of legs and two pairs of wings; the abdomen ends in anal cerci.
Respiration through ten pairs of spiracles and a branching tracheal system delivering air directly to tissues.
Excretion by Malpighian tubules emptying into the alimentary canal.
Nervous system: supra-esophageal ganglion, circum-pharyngeal ring and a ventral nerve cord with segmental ganglia.
Frog: alimentary canal ending in a cloaca, with bile and pancreatic juice entering the small intestine.
Three-chambered heart with a sinus venosus and a double circulation; respiration by buccal pumping and moist skin.
Kidneys are mesonephric with ureters opening into the cloaca, and the brain lies within a bony cranium.

items.text: Why a cockroach survives a day underwater
items.note: Tracheae deliver oxygen directly to the tissues, so the blood is not needed for gas exchange and the insect can rely on the air trapped in its tracheal system.

items.text: Why a frog inflates its throat
items.note: By lowering the floor of the mouth it draws air in, then closes the nostrils and raises the floor to push the air into the lungs — buccal pumping replaces a diaphragm.

learn.title: Organ systems and the principles that connect them

blocks.text: The specimen anatomy in this chapter is easier to hold if the systems are seen as answers to four problems that every animal must solve. Nutrition needs a tube with an opening at each end, which is the tube-within-a-tube plan: food enters at the mouth, is processed in sequence along the canal, and waste leaves separately, so processing can occur continuously rather than only at the moment of eating — one opening, as in the flatworm, forces the animal to eat and excrete through the same aperture. Transport needs a medium to carry oxygen, nutrients and waste, and the solutions range from diffusion in a sponge, through the fluid-filled coelom and haemocoel, to a closed blood system with a heart, which is what lets annelids and vertebrates sustain higher activity. Excretion must remove nitrogenous waste and maintain water balance, and the organs differ with habitat: nephridia in the earthworm, Malpighian tubules in the insect that conserve water by depositing waste as uric acid, and kidneys with a bladder in the frog. Coordination needs a fast internal network, provided by nerves conducting impulses along neurons and by hormones carried in the blood acting more slowly but over longer times — the nervous system gives the immediate response and the endocrine system sustains the slower one. In an examination answer, the marks come from linking structure to function for each system rather than from naming parts alone: write what each organ does, and the anatomy becomes an explanation rather than a list.

items: The tube-within-a-tube plan allows continuous processing with separate mouth and anus.
Transport solutions range from diffusion to a closed circulatory system with a heart.
Excretion is matched to habitat: nephridia, Malpighian tubules conserving water as uric acid, or kidneys.
Tracheae bypass the blood entirely to deliver oxygen straight to insect tissues.
Nerves give fast, short responses; hormones give slower, longer-lasting ones.
Link structure to function in every sentence, because the reasoning carries the marks.
A system fails if one part fails, which is why the parts are taught in the order food travels.

items.note: Uric acid is nearly insoluble and can be excreted as a paste with very little water, which is what lets a cockroach live in dry surroundings.
A frog withdraws its leg from a painful stimulus in milliseconds by nerve conduction, while its seasonal breeding is timed by hormones released into the blood.

keyPoints: The four animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.
Epithelia are avascular, rest on a basement membrane and regenerate rapidly.
Connective tissue is defined by a matrix secreted by its own cells.
Striated, cardiac and smooth muscle differ in control, structure and location.
The neuron, with dendrites, cell body and axon, is the unit of nervous tissue.
The earthworm has 100 to 120 segments, a clitellum at segments 14 to 16 and nephridia in each segment.
The earthworm respires through its moist body wall and has a closed circulatory system with haemoglobin.
The cockroach breathes through spiracles and tracheae and excretes through Malpighian tubules.
The frog has a three-chambered heart, buccal pumping for breathing and a cloaca for excretion and reproduction.
Organ systems are best described as answers to nutrition, transport, excretion and coordination.
Structure and function must be linked in every sentence of a descriptive answer.
Specimen identification expects both external features and the path of food through the canal.
examFocus: Tissue questions name the type, its structure, one function and one location.
Specimen anatomy expects the organs in the order food or blood travels.
Diagrams must be labelled with direction shown — anterior to posterior.
Comparative questions use the same system as the heading for each animal named.

questions.prompt: The tissue that connects muscle to bone is:
questions.explanation: A tendon is dense regular connective tissue joining muscle to bone; a ligament joins bone to bone.

questions.prompt: In the earthworm the gizzard is used for:
questions.explanation: The muscular gizzard grinds food, aided by soil particles swallowed with it, after the crop has stored it.

questions.prompt: Respiration in the cockroach takes place through:
questions.explanation: Air enters through spiracles and passes through branching tracheae directly to the tissues.

questions.prompt: Cardiac muscle differs from skeletal muscle in being:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is striated yet involuntary and branching, and it resists fatigue throughout life.

questions.prompt: The swollen region of the earthworm on segments 14 to 16 that secretes the cocoon is the __________.
questions.explanation: The clitellum is the glandular band used to identify a mature earthworm.

questions.prompt: The nitrogenous excretory organs of the cockroach, which open into the alimentary canal, are the __________ tubules.
questions.explanation: Malpighian tubules conserve water by excreting nitrogenous waste as uric acid.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and function of epithelial tissue.
questions.answer: Epithelial tissue consists of closely packed cells resting on a non-cellular basement membrane, with the free surface exposed to a cavity or the outside of the body. It has no blood supply of its own and receives nutrients by diffusion from the underlying connective tissue, and its cells divide rapidly to replace those worn away. It is classified by the number of layers, simple where there is one and stratified where there are several, and by cell shape: squamous cells are flat and form the alveoli where rapid diffusion occurs, cuboidal cells form glands and kidney tubules, and columnar cells line the intestine and absorb nutrients. Its functions follow its position — protection in the skin, absorption in the intestine, secretion in glands and conduction of mucus in the ciliated trachea.
questions.explanation: Closely packed on a basement membrane, avascular and regenerating, with layers and shapes matched to function.

questions.prompt: Why does an earthworm die when its skin dries up?
questions.answer: The earthworm has no lungs or gills, so gas exchange occurs entirely across its moist body wall. Oxygen dissolves in the film of mucus on the skin and diffuses into the blood capillaries beneath, while carbon dioxide passes out the same way. If the skin dries, oxygen can no longer dissolve and diffuse, so the worm is unable to take in oxygen and suffocates even though carbon dioxide may still escape. This dependence on a moist surface is also why earthworms are active at night and burrow into damp soil.
questions.explanation: Moist skin as the respiratory surface, the requirement for dissolved oxygen, and the consequence of drying.

questions.prompt: Name the parts of the cockroach mouthparts adapted for chewing.
questions.answer: The cockroach has biting and chewing mouthparts of five parts: the labrum forms an upper lip that covers the mouth from above, the pair of mandibles are hard and toothed for cutting and grinding food, the pair of maxillae bear sensory palps and help push food into the mouth, the labium forms a lower lip, and a median tongue-like hypopharynx lies between them. Together these parts bite off pieces of solid food and pass them inwards, which suits the cockroach as an omnivorous scavenger.
questions.explanation: Labrum, mandibles, maxillae, labium and hypopharynx, each with a line of function.

questions.prompt: Describe the alimentary canal of the earthworm from mouth to anus and explain how each part is adapted to its function.
questions.answer: Food enters the mouth in the first segment, which lies beneath the prostomium, a lobe that guides soil and organic matter inwards. The pharynx acts as a suction pump, drawing the soil in, and its muscular walls then push the food into the thin-walled oesophagus, which passes it posteriorly. The crop is a thin-walled storage chamber in which food is held temporarily before it reaches the gizzard. The gizzard has a thick muscular wall and no teeth, so it grinds the food with the help of soil particles and sand swallowed along with it, breaking up the organic matter and the mineral grains that surround it. The food then passes into the intestine, whose dorsal wall is folded inward to form the typhlosole, a ridge that greatly increases the surface area for absorption and brings blood supply close to the lumen; digested nutrients are absorbed here and passed into the blood capillaries. Undigested material continues to the rectum and is expelled through the anus as castings, which are used as manure. The single tube with two openings lets the worm feed continuously as it swallows soil, rather than having to stop and excrete through the same opening.
questions.explanation: Each organ in order with its structure and function, the typhlosole explained, and the tube plan noted.

questions.prompt: Compare the excretory organs of the earthworm, the cockroach and the frog, and explain how each is suited to the animal’s way of life.
questions.answer: The earthworm possesses nephridia, coiled tubules present in nearly every segment that open to the exterior by a nephridiopore. Nitrogenous waste filtered from the blood is passed along the tubule, and water is reabsorbed before the fluid is discharged; because the worm lives in moist soil, losing water in this dilute form is not a serious problem, and the segmental arrangement serves the segmented body plan directly. The cockroach instead has Malpighian tubules, fine thread-like tubes hanging into the gut at the junction of midgut and hindgut. They remove uric acid from the blood and empty it into the alimentary canal, from which it is expelled with the faeces; because uric acid is almost insoluble, very little water is lost, which is exactly what an insect needs to live on land without drying out. The frog, being an amphibian, has a vertebrate kidney of the mesonephric type: paired kidneys filter the blood through many nephrons, and the urine passes by ureters to a cloaca where it is stored before expulsion. Water balance is helped by the bladder, and because the frog lives near water it can afford a more dilute urine than a reptile or mammal. Each system therefore reflects the same trade-off — waste removal against water conservation — settled differently for a soil animal, a land arthropod and an amphibian.
questions.explanation: All three animals with their organs, the type of waste and the water relation, and a closing statement on the trade-off.

questions.prompt: Explain why the cockroach is described as having an open circulatory system, and give one advantage and one disadvantage of such a system.
questions.answer: An open circulatory system is one in which the blood, or haemolymph, is not confined to vessels throughout its circuit. In the cockroach a long tubular heart in the abdomen pumps haemolymph through ostia into short conducting vessels, but the fluid then empties into the body cavity, the haemocoel, and bathes the organs directly before returning to the heart. The haemolymph therefore does not travel in a closed loop of capillaries as it does in the earthworm or a frog. The advantage is economy and simplicity: no extensive network of delicate capillaries needs to be built and maintained, and the pressure required is low, so a small heart suffices for a body that is also supplied with oxygen by tracheae and does not need blood to carry it. The disadvantage is imprecision: because the haemolymph does not reach each tissue in a controlled volume, it cannot serve rapid, high-rate delivery of oxygen and nutrients during sustained activity, which limits the insect’s capacity for prolonged exertion. The tracheal system compensates for the respiratory shortfall by carrying oxygen directly to the cells.
questions.explanation: Definition with the heart and haemocoel, one advantage, one disadvantage, and the tracheal compensation noted.
